strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP evaluation problem: consistency across LLM judges alongside alignment with human judgments. The checklist framework is clearly motivated, requires no evaluator training, and exposes which criteria contribute to each score.

The experiments cover 12 evaluator models, two benchmarks, and eight evaluation dimensions. Reported average Spearman correlations improve over G-Eval for all 12 models on SummEval and 10 of 12 on Topical-Chat, providing promising evidence for the practical usefulness of checklist prompting.

The appendices provide detailed per-dimension results, seed questions, prompt templates, model identifiers, and implementation settings. The discussion also acknowledges limitations of binary judgments and failures on some low-quality texts.
weaknesses: The central agreement claim is insufficiently specified. Section 5.2 does not explain whether agreement is calculated over individual checklist answers or aggregated scores, how score categories are constructed for Fleiss’ κ, or which distance function is used for Krippendorff’s α. Agreement on binary subquestions would not directly establish comparable agreement on final text-quality scores. Furthermore, Table 8 measures variance of correlation coefficients across models, which does not substantiate the abstract’s stronger claim of reduced rating variance.

The comparison does not isolate the proposed explanation for the gains. Section 4.4 describes one sampled response at temperature 1 but does not explain whether G-Eval’s probability-based scoring is retained. Original prompts alone do not establish a faithful baseline implementation. Seed-only and decomposed-Likert controls would help distinguish benefits of binary responses from richer human-designed criteria and aggregation over multiple judgments.

Reproducibility remains materially incomplete despite the useful appendices. The manuscript supplies seed questions but not the final augmented and filtered checklists containing 111 SummEval and 105 Topical-Chat questions. Generation templates also contain unspecified conditions and examples, and no implementation or checklist artifact link is provided. These checklists define the actual evaluator; regenerating different questions would not reproduce the reported experiments.

Several numerical inconsistencies require reconciliation. In Table 11, MOVERScore’s listed dimension-level Spearman correlations average to 0.5165, whereas the reported average is 0.4740. Table 13 similarly reports BERTScore’s average Spearman correlation as 0.2520 despite component values averaging 0.3195. Table 8’s Topical-Chat Spearman and Pearson summaries are interchanged relative to Table 13. These discrepancies weaken confidence in the reported comparisons and aggregation pipeline.

The high-quality analysis is not adequately documented. Figure 3 specifies a human-score threshold of at least 3, while Table 4 identifies Topical-Chat naturalness as a 1–3 scale. Without an explained rescaling or different threshold, that subgroup would have constant gold ratings and undefined correlation. Dataset-specific thresholds, subgroup sizes, and uncertainty estimates are needed. Resolving these analysis issues and the central measurement and reproducibility gaps is necessary before a sound Findings recommendation.
